RagShortTexts: The 13th-century counterweight trebuchet replaced human traction, using multi-ton.

Variants.Content: The 13th century marked the zenith of siege engineering through the perfection of the counterpoise trebuchet. Replacing volatile human-pulled traction artillery, master carpenters mounted multi-ton earth or lead boxes onto pivoting short lever arms, primed with geared windlasses. The kinematic multiplier of a flexible rope sling hurled 200-to-300-pound dressed masonry balls across 300 yards with devastating ballistic repeatability, rendering vertical castle walls obsolete without concentric layers.

Unlike tired human pullers, a counterweight never grows sluggish. Timber-wrights cock the long arm by day, and the crew who sets the release rope crouches behind earthen mantlets, flinching at every crack of the beam. When the arm slams forward, the gunners learn to read the sound of stone meeting parapet, and a poorly aimed shot can bring the whole rampart down on the men who loaded it.
